title: Coverage of highly-cited documents in Google Scholar, Web of Science, and Scopus: a multidisciplinary comparison
extended_summary:
This paper does not match the requested 2025 secondary-school writing study. Instead, it is a bibliometric comparison study examining whether counts of highly-cited documents depend on the choice of citation database. The authors ask how many highly-cited documents identified in Google Scholar's Classic Papers are missing from Web of Science and Scopus, whether citation counts across databases are similarly ranked, and which database reports the highest citation counts.

The study analyzes 2,515 highly-cited documents published in 2006 and listed in Google Scholar Classic Papers. The authors scraped metadata from Google Scholar, then manually searched for each document in Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus using DOI or title matching. They compared database coverage across eight broad disciplinary areas, calculated proportions of missing documents, computed Spearman correlations between citation counts across sources, and compared average log-transformed citation counts with 95% confidence intervals.

There is no educational intervention, no student sample, and no writing-related treatment or outcome assessment. The context is cross-disciplinary scholarly publishing rather than schools or classrooms. The analysis focuses on database indexing practices, including whether missing documents were absent because journals or conferences were not covered, coverage was incomplete, or documents were unpublished preprints/reports.

The main conclusion is that Google Scholar has broader coverage of highly-cited documents than Web of Science and Scopus in several areas, especially Humanities, Social Sciences, and some Engineering/Computer Science fields. Citation-count rank orders between Google Scholar and the selective databases are still very strongly correlated, but Google Scholar consistently reports higher citation counts. The authors conclude that using selective databases to compute highly-cited-document indicators can bias research assessment in poorly covered fields.
quality_tier_rationale: The provided paper is a bibliometrics study about database coverage (Google Scholar, Web of Science, Scopus), not an education intervention study and not a secondary-school writing experiment. It contains no student-writing treatment, no educational outcome evaluation, and no relevant AI-in-education methodology for the requested topic.
impact_tier_rationale: This paper does not report any educational intervention impact on student writing or related learning outcomes. Therefore it provides no usable evidence of impact for the requested secondary-school AI writing-feedback topic.
